pages.title: Optimal Control
pages.rawText:
Optimal Control

    So far, feedback control design paradigm

       • given a “control system”
          (model of an actual systems)

       • goal: track a desired/reference output                                                                                                    disturbance
            (or stabilize an equilibrium)
                                                                                                                                        reference                                  input                               output
       • design input as function of output/state                            CONTROLLER                    SYSTEM

    Two ingredients are mainly missing

       • performance index

       • constraints
           (input limitations, geometric constraints,...)

    Optimization:
     theory to find “best” decision while handling constraints

                        pervasive in Engineering... and several other fields!


                     Optimal Control: combine optimization with (feedback) control!


                                              Prof. Giuseppe Notarstefano – Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning – Introduction to Optimal Control 1 |35

pages.title: Continuous-time control systems
pages.rawText:
Continuous-time control systems

    Consider the continuous-time, t ∈R, (time-varying) system

                                  ˙x(t) = f(x(t), u(t), t),     x(0) = x0     state equation

                            y(t) = h(x(t), u(t), t)                  output equation

      • x(t) ∈Rn state of the system at time t
      • u(t) ∈Rm input of the system at time t
      • y(t) ∈Rp output of the system at time t


                       x1(t)          u1(t)          y1(t) 

                           x(t) =              u(t) =               y(t) =                                                                                                                                                                             ...                                                                                             ...                                                                                            ...                                                                                               
                                 xn(t)             um(t)               yp(t)


    Remark In applications, we will mainly work with time-invariant systems, ˙x(t) = f(x(t), u(t)), even
    though time-varying ones may be considered.                               □

pages.title: Discrete-time control systems and notation
pages.rawText:
Discrete-time control systems and notation


   We consider nonlinear, discrete-time systems described by

                            x(t + 1) = f(x(t), u(t), t),     x(0) = x0,      t ∈N0

    but from now on we will use the (more compact) notation

                               xt+1 = ft(xt, ut),     x0 = x0,      t ∈N0

    where xt ∈Rn and ut ∈Rm are the state and the input of the system at time t.





                                              Prof. Giuseppe Notarstefano – Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning – Introduction to Optimal Control 8 |35
pages.text:
Discrete-time control systems and notation
We consider nonlinear, discrete-time systems described by
x(t + 1) = f(x(t), u(t), t), x(0) = x0, t ∈N0
but from now on we will use the (more compact) notation
xt+1 = ft(xt, ut), x0 = x0, t ∈N0
where xt ∈Rn and ut ∈Rm are the state and the input of the system at time t.

pages.title: Discrete-time control systems and notation
pages.rawText:
Discrete-time control systems and notation


    Consider a nonlinear, discrete-time system on a finite time-horizon

                          xt+1 = ft(xt, ut),     x0 = x0,      t = 0, . . . , T −1                     (1)

    where xt ∈Rn and ut ∈Rm are the state and the input of the system at time t.

    Notation
   We use x ∈RnT and u ∈RmT to denote, respectively, the stack of the states xt for all t = 1, . . . , T
    and the inputs ut for all t = 0, . . . , T −1, that is

                              x := col(x1, . . . , xT )
                             u := col(u0, . . . , uT −1).

    where col(x1, . . . , xT ) is the vector with components x1, . . . , xT .





                                              Prof. Giuseppe Notarstefano – Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning – Introduction to Optimal Control 9 |35
pages.text:
Discrete-time control systems and notation
Consider a nonlinear, discrete-time system on a finite time-horizon
xt+1 = ft(xt, ut), x0 = x0, t = 0, . . . , T −1 (1)
where xt ∈Rn and ut ∈Rm are the state and the input of the system at time t.
Notation
We use x ∈RnT and u ∈RmT to denote, respectively, the stack of the states xt for all t = 1, . . . , T
and the inputs ut for all t = 0, . . . , T −1, that is
x := col(x1, . . . , xT )
u := col(u0, . . . , uT −1).
where col(x1, . . . , xT ) is the vector with components x1, . . . , xT .

pages.title: System trajectories
pages.rawText:
System trajectories


    Let us introduce the definition of trajectory of a (possibly) nonlinear, discrete-time control system.

     Definition A pair (¯x, ¯u) ∈RnT × RmT  is called a trajectory of system (1) if ¯xt+1 = ft(¯xt, ¯ut) for all
     t = 0, . . . , T −1. In particular, ¯x is the state trajectory, while ¯u is the input trajectory.        □


    Let us recall a special class of trajectories characterized by constant input and constant state.

     Definition A state-input pair (xe, ue) ∈Rn×Rm is called an equilibrium pair of (1) if (xt, ut) = (xe, ue),
     t ∈N0, is a trajectory of the system.                                    □

     Equilibria of discerete-time, time-invariant systems satisfy xe = f(xe, ue).





                                            Prof. Giuseppe Notarstefano – Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning – Introduction to Optimal Control 10 |35

t = 0, . . . , T −1. In particular, ¯x is the state trajectory, while ¯u is the input trajectory. □
Let us recall a special class of trajectories characterized by constant input and constant state.
Definition A state-input pair (xe, ue) ∈Rn×Rm is called an equilibrium pair of (1) if (xt, ut) = (xe, ue),
t ∈N0, is a trajectory of the system. □
Equilibria of discerete-time, time-invariant systems satisfy xe = f(xe, ue).

pages.title: Linearization of a system about a trajectory
pages.rawText:
Linearization of a system about a trajectory


    Given the dynamics

                                     xt+1 = ft(xt, ut)      t ∈N0,

    and a trajectory (¯x, ¯u) (i.e., ¯xt+1 = ft(¯xt, ¯ut) for all t ∈N0), the linearization of (1) about (¯x, ¯u) is
     given by the linear (possibly) time-varying system

                            ∆xt+1 = At∆xt + Bt∆ut      t ∈N0,

    with At and Bt the Jacobians of ft, with respect to state and input respectively, evaluated at (¯x, ¯u).





                                            Prof. Giuseppe Notarstefano – Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning – Introduction to Optimal Control 11 |35
pages.text:
Linearization of a system about a trajectory
Given the dynamics
xt+1 = ft(xt, ut) t ∈N0,
and a trajectory (¯x, ¯u) (i.e., ¯xt+1 = ft(¯xt, ¯ut) for all t ∈N0), the linearization of (1) about (¯x, ¯u) is
given by the linear (possibly) time-varying system
∆xt+1 = At∆xt + Bt∆ut t ∈N0,
with At and Bt the Jacobians of ft, with respect to state and input respectively, evaluated at (¯x, ¯u).

pages.title: Recall some tools for nonlinear systems analysis and control
pages.rawText:
Recall some tools for nonlinear systems analysis and control


      • System Trajectories and equilibria

      • Linearization

      • Equilibrium (origin) stabilization (typically time-invariant systems)

      • Output/trajectory tracking (typically time-varying systems)


    The following issues are not handled explicitly

      • Optimize a performance index (e.g., control effort, distance from a target point, time, ...)

      •  Explicitly handle constraints (e.g., saturations on the inputs, collision/obstacle avoidance, regions
         where the state has to be confined,...)

pages.title: Optimization: main ingredients
pages.rawText:
Optimization: main ingredients


    The main ingredients of an optimization problem are

    Decision vector: z ∈Rd

    Cost function: ℓ(z) : Rd →R cost associated to decision z

     Constraints (constraint sets): for some given functions hi : Rn →R, i = 1, . . . , m, and gj : Rn →R,
    the decision vector z ∈Rd needs to satisfy

                                        hi(z) = 0      i = 1, . . . , m
                                         gj(z) ≤0     j = 1, . . . , r.

     Equivalently we can say that we require z ∈Z with

                        Z = {z ∈Rn | h(z) = 0, g(z) ≤0},

    where we compactly denoted h(z) = col(h1(z), . . . , hm(z)) and g(z) = col(g1(z), . . . , gr(z)).



                                            Prof. Giuseppe Notarstefano – Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning – Introduction to Optimal Control 13 |35

pages.title: Discrete-time optimal control: main ingredients (I)
pages.rawText:
Discrete-time optimal control: main ingredients (I)


    The main ingredients of a discrete-time optimal control problem are

    Dynamics: a (discrete-time) system in state space form

                                 xt+1 = ft(xt, ut)      t = 0, . . . , T −1

   We will mainly work on a finite horizon, i.e. 0 < T < +∞(notation: 0, . . . , T −1). In some cases we
      will also consider an infinite horizon, i.e., T = +∞.


    The dynamics introduces T equality constraints

                x1 = f(x0, u0)                          i.e.                    ft(x0, u0) −x1 = 0
                x2 = f(x1, u1)                          i.e.                    ft(x1, u1) −x2 = 0
                                                                                            ...                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      ...
              xT = f(xT −1, uT −1)                  i.e.             ft(xT −1, uT −1) −xT = 0



                                            Prof. Giuseppe Notarstefano – Optimal Control and Reinforcement Learning – Introduction to Optimal Control 18 |35

... ...

      • the velocity is close to the corresponding desired velocity profile (vdesx,t, vdesy,t) for all t = 1, . . . , T
      • angle and angular velocity, θt, ωt, are “not too high”
